transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Priya (NimblePay Eng Lead), Alex (Platform), Samir (Security), Eva (PM)

Summary: quick review of adapter bindings, structured payload contract, small runtime tuning for batching/latency, next steps for bench runs and security signoff. Some noisy lines; speaker labels occasionally generic.

Topics: adapter pattern, SDK bindings, function/tool calling semantics, structured JSON payloads, error/fallback patterns, telemetry/logging, security/KMS, bench plan.

[00:00] Maya: All right everyone, thanks for joining. we'll keep this to fifty minutes — quick sync on the adapter bindings and the structured payload contract.
[00:17] Priya: Yep, thanks. We had a couple of integration attempts this week, ran into two main issues: 1) the SDK example assumed synchronous function calls which doesn't match our async job queue, and 2) the structured JSON sometimes had extra fields the parser didn't expect.
[00:34] Jonah: mm-hmm, yeah on the SDK side we pushed an example that used the default blocking call — our bad. The adapter pattern we recommend supports both sync and async by returning either a payload or a tool invocation token.
[00:50] Alex: when you say tool invocation token, can you show me the shape? our infra needs a stable contract to route to our job queue.
[01:06] Jonah: Sure — in the sample repo the function call looks like: {"tool": "upsert_invoice", "args": {"invoice_id": "123"}} but we also have a wrapper where the SDK returns {"invoke_type": "deferred", "job_ref": "uuid-...", "payload": {...}} so the adapter can enqueue. I'll share the exact snippet.
[01:33] Priya: okay that helps. but the structured output also included a meta block that we didn't account for. the field was called summaryText and sometimes summary_text — casing mismatch.
[01:48] Eva: there's some downstream validation in our acceptor service that fails when unknown keys appear, so we need a strict schema.
[02:02] Maya: understood — we can lock down a JSON schema. proposal: top-level keys: status, result, artifacts, metadata. metadata will be an object but we can enumerate allowed subkeys.
[02:20] Samir: quick security note — if adapter returns job refs we need them to be short-lived and signed, otherwise our queue will accept anything. we prefer HMAC signed tokens or KMS-wrapped references.
[02:36] Jonah: Good point. Redwood supports signed invocation tokens and integrates with customer-managed KMS for token signing. there's a small latency hit for signature verification, typically 3-8ms per request depending on the KMS path.
[02:53] Alex: can that verification be offloaded to the job router? we don't want per-token calls to KMS from the runtime.
[03:06] Jonah: yes, you can verify once in the router layer and then issue a short-lived internal token for the runtime. we'll document the recommended flow in the repo.
[03:20] Priya: back to SDK usage: our engineers tried the Python SDK and the TypeScript one. TS had better typed bindings for function calling but returned an extra wrapper that confused our parser.
[03:35] Maya: that's likely the safety wrapper we add in the hosted SDK for automatic telemetry. we can provide a 'bare' binding that returns the raw model output without telemetry wrapper for your staging runs.
[03:49] Eva: would stripping telemetry lose tracing we rely on? we need traces to tie token usage back to customer sessions.
[03:58] Jonah: you can keep a minimal trace header while disabling the extra JSON envelope — we can show both in the example.
[04:10] Alex: latency vs batching — our initial runs used batch size 8 with a sub-second SLA target. we saw token latencies spike when KV cache warmups happened. any suggestions?
[04:26] Jonah: sounds like prefix caching mismatch. if your requests have variance in prompt length, batching amplifies KV cache misses. two approaches: 1) use session affinity so warm KV caches stay on the same GPU for a user session, or 2) adopt adaptive batching that prioritizes short sequences for low-latency routes.
[04:45] Priya: session affinity sounds attractive but our orchestrator is Kubernetes with ephemeral pods. how do you pin a session?
[04:56] Maya: Redwood's routing supports sticky routing keys — you can use user_id hash to route to the same backend slice. with Dedicated you get more control; in Hosted we'll surface a route key in the SDK.
[05:12] Alex: is affinity compatible with autoscaling? we worry about hot shards.
[05:18] Jonah: yes, the runtime rebalances gradually and migrates KV caches; there is a short window of higher latency during shard transfers. for the pilot you can reserve a small dedicated pool to avoid transfers.
[05:34] Samir: security again — we need audit logs for token issuance and adapter operations. these must be exportable to our SIEM.
[05:43] Maya: audit logs can be shipped to your cloud logging — we have structured log events for function invocations, token issuances, and KMS operations. Jonah will include sample log formats.
[05:55] Priya: ok the validation schema — can we walk through an example of a failing response so we can agree on strict keys?
[06:04] Jonah: sure — example 1: model returns {"status":"ok","result":{"text":"..."},"meta":{"summary_text":"..."}} but your parser expects summaryText under metadata.summary and fails on summary_text. Proposed stable schema: metadata.summary (string), metadata.version (string), artifacts: list of {type, url}.
[06:31] Eva: can we add a field metadata.confidence (float) for downstream routing?
[06:38] Maya: yes, add confidence. we recommend value between 0-1 and a default of null if unknown.
[06:45] Priya: what about partial outputs and streaming? some of our flows stream in tokens and we need to assemble into the final JSON. do you provide a streaming schema?
[06:58] Jonah: streaming uses chunk envelopes. each chunk is either a content_delta or a struct_complete event. we attach a chunk_id and final=true on the last chunk. we'll include an example of reassembly in the adapter repo.
[07:16] Alex: perfect. on the SDK side, what about retries — should the adapter be idempotent? our job queue dedupes based on job_ref but if the SDK retries the same call and returns a new job_ref we get duplicates.
[07:31] Jonah: SDK will emit an idempotency_key if available; the adapter should pass that through to the queue dedupe. we'll show the idempotency headers.
[07:43] Samir: for compliance we need retention controls. are generated artifacts (like logs or model outputs) stored by Redwood?
[07:52] Maya: by default hosted mode retains 30 days, but for pilot we can set retention to 7 days or disable retention if you're in Private. Dedicated/Private gives you full control and no Redwood-stored artifacts.
[08:07] Priya: we'll probably need Private for production, but pilot can start hosted with reduced retention. Samir will review legal.
[08:15] Eva: one more thing — function calling fallback. if the model suggests a tool not installed, what's the runtime behavior?
[08:25] Jonah: runtime tries to match tool names; if not found falls back to a structured stub that returns suggested_tool and confidence. you can map those to a human review queue. there's also an automatic fallback to a safe default tool you configure.
[08:43] Priya: that will help triage. can we discuss metrics we should capture during bench runs?
[08:50] Jonah: capture p50/p90 p99 latencies per endpoint, tokens per second, cache hit rate, and error rates for rejected tool calls. also capture time-to-first-byte for streaming.
[09:03] Alex: we'll include tail latencies; our SLA is 500ms p95 for interactive flows.
[09:11] Maya: noted — benchmark script will emit those metrics. Jonah will set up dashboards in the sample console.
[09:21] Priya: about the structured payload mismatch we saw — sometimes numbers were strings. our strict parsers choke on that. can you ensure type coercion rules?
[09:33] Jonah: yes we can add an optional coercion layer in the adapter — e.g., if schema expects integer and model output is string digits we coerce, else we raise validation error. The adapter can be configured strict or lenient.
[09:48] Eva: what's the recommended default for pilot?
[09:51] Maya: lenient with logged warnings. then strict for production.
[09:55] Alex: logging: are logs correlated with tokens for cost attribution? we need per-request token counts.
[10:03] Jonah: yes, token counts are emitted per request and per model. you can tie that to customer session id. we'll also show cost estimates in the console.
[10:14] Maya: quick check — samples to share after call: adapter repo, JSON schema, benchmark runbook, security docs (SOC2, KMS notes), and a short demo recording.
[10:27] Priya: sounds good. one technical ask: could we get a minimal Node adapter that uses our internal job queue (Rabbit) examples?
[10:36] Jonah: yes — Node + Python samples. Node sample will include RabbitMQ enqueue example and token verification middleware.
[10:45] Samir: on key management, we need support for customer-managed keys in AWS KMS and for GCP KMS as well. can you confirm both?
[10:56] Maya: we support AWS KMS and GCP KMS; HSM support is via Private deployments. we'll flag the exact APIs in the security doc.
[11:07] Eva: timelines: we'll do bench runs next week and aim to decide on Dedicated vs Hosted pilot by end of month.
[11:15] Maya: good. any blockers?
[11:18] Priya: staging access provisioning — Alex will send that today.
[11:22] Alex: yes I'll open a ticket with creds.
[11:25] Maya: great. Recap of next steps...
